title: Thinking, Fast and Slow
subtitle: Daniel Kahneman
description: A synthesis of decades of research distinguishing fast, intuitive judgment (System 1) from slow, effortful reasoning (System 2), and cataloguing the systematic biases that arise when the fast system is relied on for judgments it isn't well-suited for.

title: Influence: The Psychology of Persuasion
subtitle: Robert Cialdini
description: Based on Cialdini's field research working undercover in sales and fundraising organizations, this book identifies six recurring principles (reciprocity, commitment, social proof, authority, liking, scarcity) that reliably move people toward compliance.

title: Predictably Irrational
subtitle: Dan Ariely
description: A behavioral economist presents original experiments showing that people's departures from rational choice, such as anchoring on arbitrary numbers or overvaluing free things, follow consistent, predictable patterns rather than being random noise.

title: Nudge
subtitle: Richard Thaler & Cass Sunstein
description: Argues that because choices are always presented within some 'choice architecture,' that architecture can be designed to help people act on their own long-term goals (such as saving for retirement) without restricting their options.

title: The Person and the Situation
subtitle: Lee Ross & Richard Nisbett
description: A foundational social psychology text arguing, with extensive experimental evidence, that situational and social context predicts behavior far more strongly than most people intuitively credit, and that underestimating this (the fundamental attribution error) leads to persistent misjudgments of others.

title: Mistakes Were Made (But Not by Me)
subtitle: Carol Tavris & Elliot Aronson
description: Explores how cognitive dissonance drives people, including experts and public officials, to unconsciously justify their own errors and bad decisions after the fact rather than admit fault, using real cases from politics, medicine, and criminal justice.

title: The Social Animal
subtitle: Elliot Aronson
description: A long-standing introductory survey of social psychology's core findings on conformity, persuasion, prejudice, and self-justification, written for general readers by one of the field's most influential experimentalists.

title: Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases
subtitle: Edited by Daniel Kahneman, Paul Slovic & Amos Tversky
description: The original academic anthology that established the heuristics-and-biases research program, collecting the founding experimental papers on anchoring, availability, representativeness, and other mental shortcuts.

title: Sway: The Irresistible Pull of Irrational Behavior
subtitle: Ori Brafman & Rom Brafman
description: A popular-science survey of behavioral economics and social psychology phenomena, such as loss aversion and diagnosis bias, illustrated through real-world case studies including aviation accidents and business decisions.

title: 50 Great Myths of Popular Psychology
subtitle: Scott O. Lilienfeld, Steven Jay Lynn, John Ruscio & Barry L. Beyerstein
description: Written by research psychologists specifically to separate widely believed pop-psychology claims, such as the idea that we use only 10% of our brains, from what the actual research evidence supports, making it a useful corrective to the genre it belongs to.

title: Daniel Kahneman
subtitle: Psychologist; co-developed prospect theory with Amos Tversky; 2002 Nobel laureate in Economic Sciences
description: Kahneman's collaboration with Tversky founded modern behavioral economics by showing that human judgment under uncertainty systematically departs from classical rational-choice models in predictable ways.

title: Amos Tversky
subtitle: Cognitive psychologist; co-developed prospect theory and the heuristics-and-biases research program
description: Tversky and Kahneman's joint experiments identified specific mental shortcuts, such as the availability and representativeness heuristics, that explain many everyday errors in probability judgment; Tversky died in 1996, before the Nobel Prize (which is not awarded posthumously) recognized the work.

title: Robert Cialdini
subtitle: Regents' Professor Emeritus of Psychology and Marketing, Arizona State University
description: Cialdini's field research, conducted by taking jobs inside sales, advertising, and fundraising organizations to observe persuasion tactics firsthand, produced the widely cited six principles of influence that remain a standard reference in both psychology and marketing.

title: Elliot Aronson
subtitle: Social psychologist; developed the jigsaw classroom method
description: Beyond his textbook writing, Aronson designed the 'jigsaw classroom,' a cooperative-learning technique shown to reduce intergroup prejudice among schoolchildren, and conducted some of the foundational experiments on cognitive dissonance alongside Leon Festinger's original theory.

title: Leon Festinger
subtitle: Social psychologist; originated cognitive dissonance theory
description: Festinger's 1957 theory of cognitive dissonance, developed partly through his covert observation of a doomsday cult after its prophecy failed, remains one of the most influential and replicated frameworks in social psychology for explaining motivated reasoning.

title: Cognitive dissonance
description: The well-established finding that holding contradictory beliefs or acting against one's own stated values creates psychological discomfort, which people typically resolve by changing a belief, adding justifications, or discounting the conflicting evidence rather than changing the behavior.

title: Prospect theory
description: A well-supported descriptive model of decision-making under risk showing that people evaluate outcomes as gains or losses relative to a reference point, weigh losses roughly twice as heavily as equivalent gains, and treat probabilities non-linearly.

title: Confirmation bias
description: One of the most robustly replicated findings in cognitive psychology: people tend to search for, interpret, and recall information in ways that confirm what they already believe, while scrutinizing or discounting disconfirming evidence more harshly.

title: Fundamental attribution error
description: A well-documented tendency to explain other people's behavior by appeal to their personality or character while underweighting the situational pressures they faced, even though people readily invoke situational excuses for their own behavior.

title: Replication crisis in psychology
description: Since around 2011, large multi-lab replication projects have found that a substantial share of published psychology findings, including some famous classic studies, do not reproduce reliably under close replication, prompting the field to adopt preregistration and larger sample sizes; this is a genuinely important reason to hold individual studies more tentatively than headlines suggest.
